newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK to maintain own stance in WTO apart from China.
newsitem.headline: HK to maintain own stance in WTO apart from China.

text.p: Hong Kong will maintain its independence in the World Trade Organisation (WTO) even if that meant opposing China when the territory's future sovereign joins the global trade body, a senior official said on Friday.

"When China has joined the WTO, the Hong Kong delegation to the WTO will still represent Hong Kong interests and Hong Kong interests alone," Hong Kong Secretary for Trade and Industry Denise Yue told a news conference.
If the interests of the two coincided, that was fine and good, Yue said.

"But I can also envisage there will be occasions when Hong Kong's commercial interests differ from those of mainland China's. When that happens, the Hong Kong delegation will argue from the viewpoint of Hong Kong and no one else's," she said.
Such a situation would not be unfamiliar since Hong Kong now found itself occassionally in opposition to the European Union, of which current-sovereign Britain was a member, she said.

Hong Kong will remain a separate customs territory and maintain independent membership in the WTO and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum even after the British colony reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30, Yue said.

The secretary said she did not know when China would join the WTO, but said the trade group would not be complete without the giant nation and that its accession would bring benefits to Hong Kong and other trading nations.

"Hong Kong investors in mainland China will no longer be confronted with many bilateral disputes between China and the rest of the world, and in which China is unable to seek solution from the world trade organisation," she said.
Hong Kong businesses are affected when bilateral trade disputes erupt between the China and the United States, the territory's two largest trading partners.
Yue also reiterated Hong Kong would maintain its present free-trade and market-oriented policies as promised in the Basic Law, the territory's future constitution drawn up by Beijing.
China on Friday said its bid for accession to the WTO had made major progress in talks in Geneva this month but conceded that many hurdles remained.

Beijing's bid to join the trade body has been held up because it has been pushing for membership on the easier terms accorded a developing country. But some Western nations, including the United States, insist China's economy is too big for such treatment.
